The heterogeneous domain adaptation problem
Source and target examples describe related classes with different feature spaces.

Goal: transfer useful source supervision without assuming shared coordinates.
Explain that ordinary domain adaptation commonly assumes the same features. Here source and target dimensions differ, as in different image descriptors or languages. Source: paper Sections 1 and 4.
Feature augmentation
HFA learns two projections into a shared latent space, then retains domain-specific information.
Source xₛ
P xₛ
AUGMENTED VECTOR
φₛ(xₛ) = [ P xₛ ; xₛ ; 0 ]
Target xₜ

The first block is shared. The remaining blocks preserve source-only and target-only signals.
A standard max-margin classifier can operate on these vectors.
Equation 1. P maps source and Q maps target into a common subspace. The augmentation contains common features plus original source or target features, padded by zeros.
HFA optimization and kernelization
The paper replaces explicit projections with a transformation metric H.

Kernel form

Result: the final HFA objective has a global optimum under the MKL formulation.

Sections 2.3 to 2.6. Kernelization avoids dependence on the high-dimensional explicit feature spaces. H is decomposed into rank-one PSD matrices. The paper describes a cutting-plane procedure and says convergence reaches a global solution for the convex formulation.
Algorithm 1: supervised HFA
Initialize one rank-one PSD metric
Solve the current MKL problem for α and θ
Construct the most violated rank-one metric
Add the metric and repeat until convergence
Prediction uses the learned target-side kernel map and the SVM decision function.
Computational cost includes kernel square roots and repeated MKL solves.
Walk through Algorithm 1. The key insight is that the active metric is selected in closed form after the current MKL solution. The paper reports fewer than 50 iterations in practice.
SHFA adds unlabeled target data
Semi-supervised HFA jointly learns a classifier, metric, and plausible target labels.
LABELED SOURCE
Known labels
LABELED TARGET
Known labels
UNLABELED TARGET
Labels inferred
A balance constraint controls how many inferred labels are positive.
The original mixed-integer problem is relaxed by mixing feasible label candidates, then solved with a cutting-plane MKL procedure.

Section 3. SHFA uses a rho-SVM with squared hinge loss. It applies a label-balance constraint and a convex relaxation over candidate labelings. Algorithm 2 alternates MKL solving and violated-label search.
Experimental design
The paper tests object recognition, multilingual text categorization, and cross-lingual sentiment.

Baselines include target-only SVM, HeMap, DAMA, ARC-t, and T-SVM in the semi-supervised setting.
Section 4. Evaluation uses accuracy. The Office dataset repeats 20 random target sampling rounds. Reuters and sentiment use 10 rounds. Do not overstate individual numbers absent the tables.
Results and interpretation
Object recognition
HFA leads supervised baselines. SHFA benefits from unlabeled target examples.
Reuters text
HFA leads supervised baselines. SHFA improves further, especially with fewer labels.
Sentiment
HFA is generally strongest or comparable. SHFA improves on HFA in all reported targets.
The augmented original features matter: SHFA with full augmentation consistently exceeds the common-features-only variant in the reported Reuters experiments.

Paper Sections 4.2 and 4.3. Qualitative claims accurately track the authors’ discussion. The paper reports SHFA p=1.5 gains over HFA in several settings, including 1.2% and 1.6% on two Office source cases.

Limitations and discussion
HFA assumes labeled examples in both source and target domains.
The kernelized method can be costly because it scales with training-sample kernels.
SHFA depends on a reasonable class-balance prior for unlabeled target data.
Modern representation learning may reduce heterogeneity, but HFA remains a clear non-deep-learning baseline.
Practical lesson: preserve domain-specific evidence while learning only the correspondence needed for transfer.
Invite discussion. Emphasize this is a classical transfer-learning method, with a transparent optimization formulation and no deep neural network.
